title: Local strain evolution and microstructural characterisation of hydrogen-induced damage at different strain rates in dual phase (DP 780) steel
abstract: Effect of strain rate on the damage behaviour of hydrogen (H)-charged dual phase (DP 780) steel via the in-situ digital image correlation (DIC) technique is investigated in this work. Since stress concentration sites like notches are common in engineering practice, two types of uniaxial tensile tests have been carried out using smooth and notch tensile specimens for detailed analysis. The study reveals the significance of hydrogen embrittlement in DP 780 steel, as no strain rate effect is observed on the mechanical property in the case of an uncharged smooth tensile specimen. However, a significant effect of strain rate is detected after the H-charging. Hydrogen showed a lesser ability to aid the failure process when the applied strain rate is raised, as it could diffuse over a limited distance during the tensile test. The local axial and width strains, along with necking and fracture strains, are quantified for each specimen to understand the strain rate effect better. A centre-line crack is observed in every H-charged specimen's fracture surface owing to the presence of MnS inclusion in DP steel along the central line and its interaction with the atomic hydrogen. Moreover, the degree of hydrogen embrittlement is substantially higher in the notch tensile specimens than in the smooth ones.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strength steels (HSS), like dual phase (DP) steels, are often used in the automotive industry due to their exceptional blend of strength and formability. The usage of these HSSs has now been encouraged since they can ensure enhanced safety and the necessary weight reduction to comply with the strict carbon dioxide emission rules. Since DP steel has a ferrite-martensite microstructure, it has a low yield strength. However, at moderate deformation stages, the large work-hardening exponent of the DP steel makes it gain a significant tensile strength [ 1 , 2 ]. The DP steel's thermo-mechanical processing comprises the conversion of some austenite islands into martensitic phases, which determines the material's typical properties. Consequently, the equivalent strength level depends primarily on the amount of the martensitic phase and its hardness in the material's microstructure. Moreover, residual stresses are generated at the martensite-ferrite interface due to the volumetric expansion of the martensitic phase into the ferritic phase during manufacture. Hence, the soft ferrite has a high density of movable dislocations that contribute to its outstanding continuous yielding. As a result, neither the yield point phenomenon nor the creation of Lüders bands exists.

Even though HSS have outstanding mechanical properties, it is thought that they are vulnerable to hydrogen (H)-induced mechanical deterioration. The hydrogen phenomenon has also been observed to hamper the possible applications of HSS  [3] . Basically, these materials experience a significant loss of ductility in the presence of hydrogen, often known as hydrogen embrittlement (HE). Amongst HSS grades, High-Strength-Low Alloyed (HSLA), DP, and Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) steels are frequently used grades in the automobile sector, and as a result, how they interact with H has already been the subject of multiple studies  [4–9] . Depover et al.  [10]  especially considered the adverse effects of H on the mechanical behaviour of these steel grades. HSLA steel was found to have a relatively low HE sensitivity of around 8 %, which is related to the favourable existence of Nb and Ti-based carbo-nitrides. However, TRIP and DP steel's ductility decreased by around 60 % and 54 %, respectively. Duprez et al.  [11]  tested the tensile strength of these materials, both H-charged and on samples that had undergone one week of air discharge. They have concluded that the hydrogen-induced reduction in elongation for TRIP and DP steels were primarily reversible, though it was irreversible in the case of HSLA steel. Furthermore, similar findings were obtained by Escobar et al.  [12] , who studied these HSSs using thermal-desorption spectroscopy (TDS). Laureys et al. [ 6 , 7 ] performed a detailed microstructural examination of these materials in the presence of hydrogen. They revealed that fracture initiation arose in the martensite phase, particularly along the lath-martensite interface.

In addition, the fracture morphology of H-charged HSS is significantly altered by the higher hydrogen concentration, particularly in DP steels  [13–18] . The major differences in mechanical properties between DP steel's martensite and ferrite phases cause certain issues when H is present  [19] . Sudhakar et al.  [20]  reported the occurrence of transgranular fracture surfaces with some secondary cracks obtained after the H-charging of DP steel. It has been demonstrated that when martensite content in the DP steel rises, secondary cracks also increase  [21] . According to Sun et al.  [22] , DP steel experiences sub-structural changes as a result of its significantly higher susceptibility to HE. When the steel is charged with hydrogen, they found that fractures form at the lath boundaries and interface. Kumar et al.  [23]  investigated the HE phenomenon on DP 780 steel at three H-charging times, i.e., 1, 4, and 24 h. They have observed a centre-line crack in all the fracture surfaces of H-induced tensile samples irrespective of H-charging time. However, the size of the centre-line crack increases with the increase in H-charging time. They have reported that the centre-line crack appeared due to Sulphur being present in the DP steel as an impurity and forming MnS inclusions, which tend to segregate along the central line. When hydrogen is present, these MnS inclusions could trigger H-induced cracks. Recently, the effect of H-diffusion in DP steel was also seen by examining the fracture surfaces of  in-situ  hydrogenated tensile samples  [24] . The observed change from ductile to brittle fracture caused by hydrogen and the estimated H-diffusion distance completely matched each other. Koyama et al.  [25]  recently demonstrated the micro-crack formation in ferrite-martensite DP steel when H was present. They discovered that H substantially influences the process of damage development. It was suggested that the H-enhanced localised plasticity (HELP) and H-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) mechanisms have a role in the crack growth in DP steel that resulted in an unexpected HE failure.

Generally, micro-damages, such as micro-cracks or voids generates from inclusions in ductile materials. On the contrary, the damage-initiating process in DP steels is related to localised plastic strain at a ferrite-martensite interface or within the martensite [ 26 , 27 ]. For instance, a strain localisation site in the ferrite close to the ferrite-martensite interface causes the evolution of micro-damages at the interface and the interior of martensite  [28–30] . Additionally, three regimes describe micro-damage development behaviour: damage incubation, damage progression, and damage arrest [ 31 , 32 ]. All three regimes are linked to local deformation inside the material. Therefore, a blend of plastic damage initiation resistance and damage progression arrestability determines the total elongation of DP steel.

In the case of DP steel, hydrogen must significantly impact the ability to withstand damage initiation and stop damage progression. Particularly, localised plasticity [ 33 , 34 ], hydrogen-enhanced decohesion [ 35 , 36 ], and accelerated lattice defect formation [ 37 , 38 ] can all worsen damage initiation resistance. The brittleness or plasticity limit at the crack tip controls the damage growth arrestability, making it susceptible to hydrogen's harmful effects [ 39 , 40 ]. DP steels are vulnerable to hydrogen embrittlement, which is associated with the growth of damage based on plasticity  [41] . The dynamics of hydrogen damage and hydrogen-dislocation interactions play a significant role in understanding how hydrogen affects the genesis of microstructural damage. In other words, the nature of hydrogen-induced damage progression is highly affected by the strain rate, as it influences the time for hydrogen segregation/diffusion at a certain location in the microstructure or at the crack tip.

Moreover, it was recently discovered that the strain rate greatly impacts a DP steel's susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement [ 42 , 43 ]. They have reported that the susceptibility to HE has risen with decreasing strain rate. Despite several investigations, the reason why the H-induced microstructural damage behaviour varies according to the strain rate is still unclear and needs to be explored. In the present work, strain rate sensitivity on the H-induced microstructural damage behaviour of DP 780 steel has been investigated thoroughly. Furthermore, hydrogen atoms severely impact stress concentration sites like notches  [44] , which is very common in engineering practice. Therefore, two types of uniaxial tensile tests have been carried out to understand better the fracture mechanism using smooth and notch tensile samples with and without hydrogenation, at different strain rates and H-charging times. The associated microstructure has been studied in detail to further comprehend the underlying mechanics of fracture.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
Cold-rolled dual-phase (DP 780) steel of thickness 1 mm is utilised in this study. The summary of DP steel's mechanical properties and chemical compositions are provided in  Tables 1 
                       and  2 
                      , respectively. Both smooth and notch tensile samples are prepared across the rolling direction (RD); the same geometry is shown in  Fig. 1 
                      (a). Various parametric combination sets (as-received and hydrogenated at different strain rates) for smooth and notch tensile samples are divided into twelve groups, specified in  Tables 3 
                       and  4 
                      . The tensile specimens are exposed to hydrogen without incurring any structural damage. It is accomplished via cathodic charging through a direct current (DC) power source at a constant current density of 20 mA/cm 2 . The electrolyte contains 0.5 M H2SO 4  solution, 1 g/l of thiourea, and deionised water as a solvent. Here, the anode (concurrent electrode) is a platinum wire with a diameter of 1 mm, and the cathode is a tensile specimen (working electrode). Prior to H-charging, specimens' surfaces are first ground to 2500 grit size emery paper and then washed in an ultrasonic cleaner using acetone to eliminate contaminants. All experiments are carried out at an ambient conditions.

After H-charging, some specimens are used for microstructural purposes, and others are immediately put through a uniaxial tensile test without any substantial delay ( Tables 3  and  4 ). A universal testing machine (UTM) [BISS manufacture] is employed for all tensile tests, with strain rates ranging from 10 − 
                      
                         5 
                       to 10 −3  /s. The uniaxial tensile test of smooth tensile specimens (both H-charged and uncharged) was carried out at the strain rates of 10 −5 , 10 −4 , and 10 −3  /s, whereas, in the case of notched tensile specimens, the equivalent displacement rates were set to be 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1 mm/min. This study specifies the yield stress (YS) for smooth tensile specimens as 0.2 % proof stress. The  in-situ  digital image correlation (DIC) approach is utilised to quantify the local strain evolution throughout the uniaxial tensile test. Approximately 2000 pictures are taken for each tensile test for further processing. Before the test, tensile specimens' surfaces are sprayed with black and white aerosol paint to create speckle patterns. The microstructural characteristics of each specimen, both as-received and after being hydrogenated are observed under a scanning electron microscope (SEM) [ZEISS Gemini500]. The top surfaces of the samples are polished and then etched as per conventional metallographic procedure to analyse the microstructure and quantify the micro-cracks. Further analysis of the fracture surfaces of the failed tensile specimens is done using SEM micrographs.

sections.heading: Results and discussions
paragraphs: The usual microstructure of DP 780 steel is observed using an SEM under as-received and different hydrogenated conditions. As seen in  Fig. 1 (b), the base metal's (specimen A) microstructure comprises islands of the martensitic phase scattered throughout the ferritic phase. The microstructure shows a sub-continuous martensite network with intermittent ferrite amongst martensite phases. DP steels have a microstructure that results in lower yield-to-tensile strength ratios, continuous yielding tendency, no room temperature ageing impact, and greater initial work hardening rate and tensile strength. These attributes are primarily influenced by the martensitic phase's distribution, size, and volume fraction  [45] . In specimen A, the average grain sizes of martensite and ferrite are around 3 and 6 μm, respectively. The volume fraction of the martensite is 28 %. These characteristics (average grain size and volume fraction) are almost similar in the microstructure of all the H-charged specimens as well, irrespective of varying H-charging time, as these specimens did not experience any heat treatment effect during hydrogenation.

To investigate the strain rate effect on the H-induced microstructural damage behaviour of DP 780 steel, both the smooth and notch tensile specimens are tested in various parametric combination sets. Smooth tensile specimens are divided into six groups from specimens A to F ( Table 3 ). Specimens A, B, and C are in as-received condition without hydrogenation and are put through a uniaxial tensile test at respective strain rates of 10 −5 , 10 −4 , and 10 −3  /s. In order to compare the outcomes of specimen C with those of the smooth tensile H-charged and uncharged specimens, the former is also used as a reference specimen. In DP 780 steel, Kumar et al.  [23]  investigated the impact of pulsed electric current on hydrogen-induced damage recovery. The smooth tensile specimens of DP 780 steel have been first hydrogenated for three different H-charging times, i.e., 1, 4, and 24 h to analyse the mechanical degradation behaviour thoroughly. According to their findings, when evaluated at a constant strain rate of 10 −3  /s, the specimen that had been hydrogenated for 24 h showed the greatest reduction in elongation, preceded by such that had been hydrogenated for 4 h and 1 hour. Moreover, significant degradation in the mechanical properties was detected for the specimen that was hydrogenated for 4 h. Therefore, the current study has chosen 4 h of H-charging time to investigate further the strain rate sensitivity of H-induced smooth tensile specimens.

The engineering stress-strain curves for specimens A, B, and C are shown in  Fig. 2 
                      . No impact of strain rate variation is observed on the stress-strain curves of as-received smooth tensile specimens. The yield stress (YS), ultimate tensile stress (UTS), total elongation (TEL), and uniform elongation (UEL) of all three specimens are 542 MPa, 858 MPa, 16.2 %, and 10.3 %, respectively. These similarities between the mechanical properties can also be confirmed through the fractographic examination of failed tensile specimens A, B, and C, presented in  Fig. 3 
                      . As can be seen in  Fig. 3 , a similar kind of fracture surface is obtained in all three specimens irrespective of strain rate variation. A significant degree of necking is observed in all three fracture specimens, which suggests a ductile failure mode. Due to plastic instability brought on by the growth of micro-voids and coalescence, the ultimate rupture starts from the centre. A magnified image of the fracture surfaces reveals the formation of dimples both at the centre and edge. It is noted that the centre's dimples are larger compared to those at the edge. This suggests that the coalescence of micro-voids starts from the specimens' centre. The fracture surface of the smooth tensile specimen A analysed at the lowest strain rate, i.e., 10 −5  /s, also showed some bigger voids.

However, a significant effect of strain rate variation is observed in the engineering stress-strain curves of H-charged smooth tensile specimens. In this experiment, specimens D, E, and F are H-charged for 4 h before being put through a uniaxial tensile test with respective strain rates of 10 −5 , 10 −4 , and 10 −3  /s. The engineering tensile stress-strain curves for specimens D, E, and F are illustrated in  Fig. 4 
                      (a). After hydrogenation for 4 h, all the smooth tensile specimens showed a substantial loss in ductility. Moreover, elongation of the H-charged smooth tensile specimens decreases by decreasing the strain rate. The TEL of specimens D, E, and F reduced to 5 %, 6.5 %, and 8 %, respectively. At a strain rate of 10 −5  /s, the difference in the TEL of uncharged specimen A (16 %) and H-charged specimen D (5 %) is around 11 %, which is too much for a component to undergo a catastrophic failure.  Fig. 4 (b) compares the tensile properties of specimens D, E, and F. Despite the fact that the H-charging has less impact on the material's YS and UTS, still YS of the H-charged specimens D, E, and F reduced from 542 MPa to around 512 MPa, and UTS reduced from 858 MPa to 720, 780, and 788 MPa, respectively, when compared to as-received specimen C tested at a strain rate of 10 −3  /s. The H-charged specimen tested under the lowest strain rate of 10 −5  /s (specimen D) exhibits the most significant reduction in elongation, followed by those tested at 10 −4  /s (specimen E) and 10 −3  /s (specimen F). These findings demonstrate that a decrease in the strain rate leads to an increase in the mechanical properties degradation of hydrogenated specimens.

A decrease in elongation after H-charging is most likely caused by one or more of the following factors: a reduction in local shear stress  [35] , a rise in the nucleation of dislocations and their mobility at stress concentration sites [ 35 , 46 ], a decrease in the bond strength  [47] , and an increment in the formation of vacancies  [48] . As a result, less energy is required to cause a fracture. Particularly in ferrite-martensite DP steel, it is believed that HEDE (hydrogen-enhanced decohesion) and HELP (hydrogen-enhanced localised plasticity) mechanisms play a major role in the advancement of damage inside the material, giving rise to unexpectedly early HE failure, which eventually results in a reduction in elongation  [10] .

Moreover, in the context of the strain rate sensitivity of DP 780 steel to HE susceptibility, the resistance to HE decreased at a lower strain rate. This phenomenon is attributed to the H-diffusion distance, which increases with a decrease in the strain rate, as discussed in [ 25 , 49 ]. Where ' a'  is the diffusion distance in centimetres (cm), ' t'  is the tensile test time in seconds (s), and ' D'  is the diffusion coefficient in cm 2 /s. Avramovic-Cingara et al.  [2]  determined that a comparable DP steel's diffusion coefficient was around 7.46 × 10 −7  cm 2 /s. Therefore, during the uniaxial tensile test, from the beginning of deformation till failure, the hydrogen atoms are capable of diffusing over around 204, 118, and 32 μm for respective strain rates of 10 −5  /s (specimen D), 10 −4  /s (specimen E) and 10 −3  /s (specimen F). After the onset of a micro-crack or a zone characterised by stress concentration sites during the uniaxial tensile test, atomic hydrogen may diffuse to this region to speed up the final fracture. Hydrogen indicated a lesser ability to aid the failure process when the applied strain rate is raised, as it could diffuse over a limited distance during the tensile test. This could be the reason why the ductility reduction of H-charged specimens increases with the decrease in the strain rate as the duration for H-diffusion during the tensile test increases.

The fracture surfaces of hydrogenated smooth tensile specimens D, E, and F tested at varied strain rates are depicted in  Fig. 5 
                      . A minimal reduction in area is observed for the hydrogenated specimens when compared to uncharged specimens ( Fig. 3 ). The fracture surfaces of all three hydrogenated specimens acquire a more brittle characteristic than ductile, unlike the fracture surfaces of the uncharged specimens. A brittle zone is detected at both edges, which extends nearly equivalent to the H-diffusion distance calculated for the respective specimens aforementioned. The crack is initiated from the brittle surface at the edge in all the H-charged specimens. When looking more closely, a subcritical crack spread through a shearing-like mechanism at the edge of specimen D (10 −5  /s), showcasing a pure brittle fracture in  Fig. 5 (d). Whereas both dimples and flat surfaces are observed in the middle of the fracture surface, indicating a mixture of ductile and brittle fracture zone ( Fig. 5 (e)). At a strain rate of 10 −4  /s, a combination of quasi-cleavage with a tearing-like phenomenon is obtained at the edge, representing a brittle fracture mode but less brittle than in the case of 10 −5  /s. As shown in  Fig. 5 (h), the edge of specimen F (10 −3  /s) reveals a transition zone of brittle-to-ductile fracture because the H-diffusion distance, in this case, is very less compared to specimens D and E. However, small dimples and large voids are found in the middle of specimens E and F, an indication of pure ductile failure mode.

In addition, all of the H-charged smooth tensile specimens show a centre-line crack perpendicular to the fracture surface, as seen in  Fig. 5 (a, b, and c). The specimen analysed at the lowest strain rate of 10 −5  /s appears to have this centre-line crack more evident, followed by 10 −4  /s and 10 −3  /s. The primary cause behind the formation of the centre-line crack is sulphur impurities in the DP steel. These impurities later form MnS inclusions, which tend to disperse in the central line of the DP steel  [50] . Additionally, if hydrogen is present, these MnS inclusions can cause an H-induced crack to propagate through the central line of the specimen [ 50 , 51 ]. A detailed characterisation of the centre-line crack on the fracture surface of 4 h H-charged smooth tensile specimens E is shown in  Fig. 6 
                      . SEM revealed some second-phase particles on the fracture surface along the central segregation line ( Fig. 6 a), and EDX analysis verified that they were MnS inclusions ( Fig. 6 b). The size of the MnS inclusion in  Fig. 6  is around 2 μm. Depover et al. [ 52 , 53 ] noticed a similar type of centre-line crack in the fracture surface of H-charged DP 600 steel. They demonstrated their experiments in different tensile conditions, i.e., as-received, dynamic, and static. Irrespective of the tensile condition, all the hydrogenated showed a centre-line crack. A similar fracture line may also be seen in the DP steel that has been charged with the plasma H-charging technique  [53] . In the fracture surface of DP steel, they found MnS inclusions as second-phase particles, considered highly detrimental in hydrogen presence. These inclusions were found to be segregated near the hydrogen-induced centre-line cracks. Furthermore, H-induced cracking results from hydrogen accumulation at the central line, which occurs when the sample's total hydrogen content is saturated.

An irregular local decrease in the specimen's cross-sectional area during tensile deformation is referred to as localised necking. When the necking process begins, all of the specimen's strain starts to concentrate in this area. As the tensile deformation progress, the strain rate in the region away from the neck zone gradually declines and eventually vanishes  [54] . The state of stress is triaxial near the necking zone because of the geometrical changes that take place during necking. Local strain and stress in the specimen's neck zone increase when the cross-sectional area decreases. Furthermore, micro-voids' formation causes a rapid degradation in the material's properties and damage growth, ultimately leading to the final fracture  [55] . The global and local strain components for all uniaxial smooth tensile specimens (both as-received and hydrogenated) are measured using the  in-situ  digital image correlation (DIC) technique. The measurement procedure to ascertain the strain components employs a high-contrast random dots pattern on the specimens' surface. These patterns are made by spraying a thin coating of sticky, flexible, matte white paint on the upper surface of the specimen. Afterwards, fine dots of black paint are speckled to the background.

The results of its data analysis of an as-received DP 780 steel specimen C, tested at a strain rate of 10 −3  /s, are displayed in  Fig. 7 
                       for reference.  Fig. 7 (a) depicts the specimen's local axial strain ( Ɛ 
                      yy ) contour map for various global strain values. This figure shows how the local strain component evolved at various levels during the uniaxial tensile test. The local strain development for various global strain values is captured by drawing a vertical line across the gauge length's midsection. The DaVis software supplied by LaVision is used to do this analysis.  Fig. 7  (b and d) illustrates the development of local axial ( Ɛ 
                      yy ) and width ( Ɛ 
                      xx ) strains at different global engineering strain levels throughout the uniaxial tensile test of the specimen. The local strain distribution is uniform along the specimen's gauge section until UEL, after which it is localised into a plastically deformed neck zone, as can also be seen in  Fig. 7 (a). This phenomenon is typically termed as necking. Generally, two forms of neck creation are seen when a flat sample is put through a uniaxial tensile test  [56] . Localised in-plane deformation occurs at the onset of necking, known as diffuse necking. Local necking follows diffuse necking and is an out-of-plane localised deformation that lasts until the specimen's fracture point.

The beginning of diffuse necking and the subsequent large plastic deformation in the neck zone can clearly be distinguished by a sharp increase in the curves, as exposed in  Fig. 7  (b and d). In contrast to global strain, local axial and width strain components rapidly accumulate inside the neck zone as the necking process evolves. However, when the tensile test proceeded further, the local strain components in the remaining gauge section outside the neck zone remained constant. Similar findings regarding the local strain development have already been reported by several authors [ 56 , 57 ]. The strain components are uniformly dispersed over the gauge section in the initial stages of the uniaxial tensile test. The curves get further apart from one another as the necking process continues forward ( Fig. 7  (b and d)). The local axial strain ( Ɛ

                      (a). The shift in the maximum strain localisation spot with strain rate can be attributed to the hydrogen embrittlement of DP 780 steel specimens. In the case of the uncharged specimen C (Base metal), the maximum strain localisation is typically observed near the centre of the gauge length (as indicated by the green curve in  Fig. 8 a). However, after hydrogen charging of specimens D, E, and F, the maximum strain localisation spot shifts away from the centre. This shift occurs because the onset of necking or strain localisation begins in the hydrogen embrittled specimen, where hydrogen accumulation takes place. Consequently, the maximum strain localisation spot can occur anywhere within the gauge length of a hydrogen embrittled specimen.

Furthermore, the uniaxial tensile test of uncharged and hydrogenated notched tensile specimens has also been carried out at different H-charging times and varied displacement rates to better understand HE and fracture mechanisms in DP 780 steel. For this purpose, notched tensile specimens are divided again into six groups from specimens G to L with different testing parameters, as specified in  Table 4 . Specimen G is an uncharged notched tensile specimen tested in an as-received condition at a 0.1 mm/min displacement rate. In order to compare the outcomes of specimen G with those of the notched tensile H-charged samples, the former is also used as a reference specimen. Specimens H, I, and J are first H-charged for 4, 12, and 24 h, respectively, and then put through a uniaxial tensile test at a constant displacement rate of 0.1 mm/min.

The nominal stress versus extension curves for notched tensile specimens G, H, I, and J are shown in  Fig. 9 
                      . The yield and maximum nominal stress of specimen G are 720 MPa and 975 MPa, respectively, whereas the total extension is 0.73 mm. However, a significant ductility loss is observed after the H-charging of the notched tensile specimens. The total extension of hydrogenated specimens H, I, and J are reduced to 0.57, 0.45, and 0.38 mm, respectively. Although hydrogenation has little effect on the material's tensile strength, the maximum nominal stress of the H-charged specimens decreases substantially with an increase in H-charging time, yet, it does not affect yield nominal stress much. A slight reduction in yield nominal stress is observed only in the case of 24 h H-charged specimen J. Whereas the total nominal stress of these specimens reduced to 842, 805, and 700 MPa, respectively, compared to uncharged specimen G. The reason behind the H-induced mechanical degradation of notched tensile specimens could be the same as discussed above in the case of smooth tensile specimens. However, notch tensile specimens exhibit a higher degree of hydrogen embrittlement than smooth tensile specimens do. The reason is the high triaxial state of stress realised at the notch tip of a notched tensile specimen, which does not appear in the smooth tensile specimen. Especially in the interior of the notch, the hydrostatic stress gradient in the plain strain state produces hydrogen accumulation at the tip of the notch, which speeds up the emergence of H-induced cracking  [59] .

The specimen H-charged for 24 h exhibits the highest drop in elongation, followed by specimens charged for 12 h and 4 h. These findings indicate that mechanical property deterioration increases as the H-charging time increases. This is due to the rise in the hydrogen content with increasing H-charging time, leading to more H-induced damages [ 12 , 51 ]. Zhu et al.  [60]  performed the HE phenomenon on HSS for various H-charging times. Their experimental outcomes showed that the hydrogen concentration rises and the material's ductility reduces when the H-charging period is longer. Kumamoto et al.  [43]  investigated the strain rate sensitivity in H-assisted damage evaluation in DP steel. They have revealed that the specimen's diffusible hydrogen concentration rises with time until saturation occurs.

Fig. 10 
                       depicts the scanning electron micrograph of the top surfaces of fractured H-charged notched tensile specimens H, I, and J, charged for 4, 12, and 24 h, respectively. The green arrow denotes the fracture tip of the specimens, whereas the red arrow indicates the cracks/voids formed on the top surface near the fracture tip. It looks like the material is eroded from the surface in the cracked region during hydrogenation. The maximum number of such cracks are present on the surface of the specimen hydrogenated for 24 h (Sp-J), succeeded by that hydrogenated for 12 h (Sp-I) and 4 h (Sp-H). The cracks present on the top surface of specimen J are more significant in size when compared to specimens H and I. However, the crack tip is blunt, and no trace of crack propagation line initiated from the crack tip is observed for specimen J. Whereas for specimen I, a series of crack networks can be seen, which originates from the different crack tips of the main crack. At the top surface of specimen H, the crack size is much smaller than the others, and only one crack propagation line is detected, which originates from the single crack tip of the main crack. When closely examining the magnified images of specimens H and I, an intergranular cracking is observed in both specimens ( Fig. 10 b and c). The cracks propagate from the crack tip through the ferrite-martensite intersection/grain boundary.

Furthermore, the fractography of failed tensile specimens G, H, I, and J are presented in  Fig. 11 
                      . The fracture surface of as-received notched tensile specimen G (uncharged) is almost similar to the fracture surface of as-received smooth tensile specimen B ( Fig. 3 b). A minor degree of necking is observed in the fractured specimen, less than those of the uncharged smooth tensile specimens. Due to plastic instability brought on by the stress concentration at the notches, the ultimate rupture starts from the edge. A magnified image at the centre of the fracture surfaces reveals the emergence of dimples and large voids, which suggests a ductile fracture mode ( Fig. 11 a). Though, a mixture of shearing is obtained along with small dimples at the edge. This indicates that the fracture is initiated from the notch and propagates toward the centre.

However, the fracture surfaces of hydrogenated specimens H, I, and J acquire more brittle characteristics than ductile, unlike the fracture surfaces of the uncharged specimen G. But then again, a clear difference between the fracture surfaces of all three H-charged notched tensile specimens can be observed in  Fig. 11 (b,c,d). The magnified view of the edges shows a complete brittle fracture. Though, with increasing H-charging time, the brittleness of the fracture surfaces increases. The degree of hydrogen embrittlement is maximum in the case of specimen H-charged for 24 h (Sp-J), succeeded by that charged for 12 h (Sp-I) and 4 h (Sp-H). The central region of the fracture surfaces is still ductile in specimens H and I. Whereas a mixture of ductile and brittle fracture is found in the central part of specimen J's fracture surface ( Fig. 11 d). This implies that hydrogen atoms diffuse through the thickness to the central region.

Moreover, each of the three H-charged specimens H, I, and J, exhibits a centre-line crack that runs perpendicular to the fracture surface. This is due to the presence of MnS inclusion in DP steel and its interaction with the atomic hydrogen along the central line, as discussed in the case of H-charged smooth tensile specimens ( Fig. 5 ).

Furthermore, 4 h of H-charging time has been selected to investigate further the strain rate sensitivity of H-induced notched tensile specimens. Notched tensile specimens K, L, and H are first H-charged for 4 h and then subjected to a uniaxial tensile test at different displacement rates of 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1 mm/min, respectively. The nominal stress versus extension curves for specimens K, L, and H are shown in  Fig. 12 
                      (a). After hydrogenation, all the notched tensile specimens show a significant loss in ductility. The elongation of the H-charged notched tensile specimens decreases more by decreasing the displacement rate. The total extension of specimens K, L, and H are reduced to 0.39, 0.48, and 0.57 mm, respectively. In the context of strain rate sensitivity of notched tensile specimens to HE susceptibility, the resistance to HE decreased at a lower displacement rate. This phenomenon is attributed to the H-diffusion distance, which increases with decreasing displacement rate, as aforementioned in the case of smooth tensile specimens.

The tensile properties of specimens K, L, and H are compared in  Fig. 12 (b). The maximum nominal stress of the H-charged notched specimens is also reduced with decreasing displacement rate, yet, it does not affect the yield nominal stress of the material. The maximum nominal stress of specimens K, L, and H reduced from 975 MPa to 765, 850, and 900 MPa, respectively, when compared to the as-received specimen G. The greatest decline in ductility is witnessed for the hydrogenated notched specimen tested at the lowest displacement rate of 0.001 mm/min (specimen K), followed by those tested at 0.01 mm/min (specimen L) and 0.1 mm/min (specimen H). These results show that a decrease in the displacement rate leads to a rise in the degradation of mechanical properties of notched tensile hydrogenated specimens. When a hydrogenated notched component is subjected to an external load for an extended length of time, hydrogen atoms diffuse along the steel microstructure and gather in the stress concentration zone ahead of the notch (high triaxiality)  [61] . As hydrogen accumulates in this region, a threshold hydrogen concentration may be achieved, leading to embrittlement mechanisms that cause an early failure. In the same context, several authors [ 62 , 63 ] suggested that the mobile hydrogen during the tensile deformation may also diffuse to highly stressed areas in front of the notch tip, aiding in crack growth. Stress can allow even temporarily trapped diffusible hydrogen to escape and become mobile, while tensile stress causes microstructural flaws that lead to the formation of additional trapping sites. According to their findings, a precipitate's or inclusion's tip may have a high-stress concentration. As a consequence, a triaxial field of stress may be developed, into which H-diffusion will occur even more rapidly. Atomic hydrogen has the time to do this more proficiently at lesser strain rates.

The degradation in the mechanical properties has been confirmed through the detailed SEM observation of the fracture surfaces. The SEM micrograph of 4 h H-charged notch tensile specimens K and L, tested at a displacement rates of 0.001 and 0.01 mm/min, respectively, are presented in  Fig. 13 
                      . Earlier, at a higher displacement rate in specimen H (0.1 mm/min), there was a clear distinction between the fracture surfaces at the centre and edge. Its fracture surface showed a pure brittle appearance at the edge and ductile failure at the centre, as shown in  Fig. 11 (b). In contrast, the fracture surface of H-charged specimens tested at a relatively lower displacement rates, i.e., 0.001 and 0.01 mm/min, displayed no obvious distinction between the fracture surfaces at the centre and edge. Since hydrogen atoms penetrate the specimen from all sides, it follows that during the tensile test, hydrogen diffuses along a bigger portion of the entire thickness, particularly in specimen K (0.001 mm/min). This might make it more difficult to distinguish between the H-influenced and unaffected regions in the fracture surfaces, as was the case for the lower displacement rate. The surfaces look pure embrittled both at the edge as well as at the centre. However, the fracture surface of H-charged specimen K (0.001 mm/min) exhibits shear characteristics ( Fig. 13 a), whereas a deep quasi-cleavage brittle fracture is observed ( Fig. 13 b) in the fracture surface of H-charged specimen L (0.01 mm/min). In addition, the degree of hydrogen embrittlement in H-charged notched tensile specimens is even more than that in the case of H-charged smooth tensile specimens.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The strain rate sensitivity of hydrogen (H) embrittled DP 780 steel on mechanical and microstructural damage behaviour has been investigated thoroughly in the present study. Two types of uniaxial tensile tests have been carried out using smooth and notched tensile specimens for detailed analysis. The following conclusion has been drawn from the study: 
                         
                            1. 
                            Negligible effect of strain rate variation is observed on the smooth tensile specimens of uncharged (as-received) DP 780 steel. After hydrogenation, strain rate sensitivity is observed in both smooth and notched tensile specimens. The ductility of hydrogen embrittled smooth as well as notched tensile specimens decreases with decreasing strain/displacement rate. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The lowest local axial and width strains are achieved for the hydrogenated smooth tensile specimen D, tested at the minimum strain rate, i.e., 10 −5 /s, followed by 10 −4 /s (specimen E) and 10 −3 /s (specimen F). The same sequence goes for major necking and fracture strains as well. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The degradation in the mechanical properties of the notched tensile specimen rises with increasing H-charging time. The formation of deep cracks with intergranular cracking at the ferrite-martensite interface is also observed on the top surface of the hydrogenated specimen. Its number and size rise with increasing H-charging time. A centre-line crack is revealed in all the H-charged specimens' fracture surfaces due to MnS inclusion in DP steel along the central line and its interaction with the atomic hydrogen, which is detrimental to H-induced cracking. The fractographs of H-charged specimens showed a more brittle appearance with decreasing strain rate. Moreover, the degree of hydrogen embrittlement is substantially higher in the notched specimens than in the smooth ones.
